question: Highest and best use is defined as the reasonably probable use of a property that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and:
choice_a: Maximally productive, yielding the highest value among the qualifying uses
choice_b: Least costly to construct or develop
choice_c: Preferred by the current owner, regardless of the other three tests
choice_d: Consistent with the property's original historical use
explanation: Highest and best use is the reasonably probable use of vacant land or an improved property that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive -- the use that yields the greatest net return or value, forming the foundation for every value estimate an appraiser develops.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- highest and best use), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An appraiser is valuing a small, deteriorated single-family home on a large lot in a rapidly commercializing corridor. Vacant land value for retail development exceeds the home's value as currently improved, and retail use is legally permitted, physically possible, and financially feasible on the site. Under highest and best use analysis, the appraiser should conclude that the site's highest and best use is:
choice_a: As vacant land for retail development, even though this requires demolishing the existing improvement
choice_b: Continued use as a single-family residence, since the home is still habitable
choice_c: Whatever use the appraiser personally finds most attractive
choice_d: Fixed permanently at the property's current zoning classification, regardless of market demand
explanation: When the value of land as though vacant for a different use exceeds the property's value as currently improved, and that alternative use satisfies all four highest and best use tests, the highest and best use is the higher-value alternative use -- even where it requires removing an existing structure that no longer represents the property's most productive use.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- highest and best use), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A homeowner builds a large custom estate home that substantially exceeds the size and quality of every other home in an otherwise modest, uniform subdivision. Appraisal theory holds that the value of this home relative to its construction cost will most likely be affected by the principle of:
choice_a: Conformity -- excessive nonconformity with the surrounding homes tends to suppress the value the market will support for the oversized home
choice_b: Anticipation
choice_c: Substitution
choice_d: Increasing returns
explanation: The principle of conformity holds that property value is maximized when a reasonable degree of homogeneity exists among neighboring properties; a home that greatly exceeds the size, quality, or cost of its surroundings typically cannot recapture its full cost in value, since regression pulls its value down toward the neighborhood norm.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- conformity), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A homeowner spends $45,000 installing an in-ground swimming pool, but a subsequent appraisal indicates the pool adds only about $18,000 to the property's market value. This gap between cost and value added illustrates the principle of:
choice_a: Contribution -- an improvement's value is measured by what it adds to overall property value, not by what it cost to install
choice_b: Substitution
choice_c: Balance
choice_d: Regression
explanation: The principle of contribution holds that the value of any individual improvement is measured by the amount it adds to the total property value, not by its cost of installation; a pool, kitchen remodel, or other feature can easily cost far more than it contributes, particularly where the improvement is atypical for the local market.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- contribution), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Appraisal theory recognizes that neighborhoods move through predictable life-cycle stages -- growth, stability (equilibrium), decline, and revitalization -- reflecting real estate's constant state of flux. This concept is known as the principle of:
choice_a: Change
choice_b: Anticipation
choice_c: Conformity
choice_d: Progression
explanation: The principle of change holds that no physical or economic condition remains constant; property and neighborhood values are always in transition through recognizable life-cycle stages, and an appraiser's value opinion is only valid as of a specific effective date because conditions will continue evolving afterward.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- change), Pearson VUE #094401

question: The principle holding that property value is maximized when the agents of production -- land, labor, capital, and management/entrepreneurial coordination -- exist in proper proportion to one another is the principle of:
choice_a: Balance
choice_b: Contribution
choice_c: Substitution
choice_d: Highest and best use
explanation: The principle of balance holds that value is created and sustained when the four agents of production are properly proportioned -- for example, a subdivision with too many similar-sized lots and too little supporting retail/amenity development may fail to reach its full potential value.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- balance), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An investor purchases two adjoining undersized lots, neither independently buildable under current zoning, and combines them into one conforming, buildable parcel worth more than the sum of the two lots' separate values. The act of combining the parcels is called:
choice_a: Assemblage, and the resulting increase in combined value is called plottage
choice_b: Partition
choice_c: Subdivision
choice_d: Escheat
explanation: Assemblage is the act of combining two or more separately owned parcels into one larger tract; plottage is the term for the increment of value created when the assembled tract is worth more than the sum of the individual lots' separate values -- a direct application of the highest and best use and contribution principles.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.A.3 (principles of value -- assemblage and plottage), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An appraiser inspecting a home notes peeling exterior paint and worn carpet -- both inexpensive to fix relative to the value restored -- alongside a cracked foundation slab whose repair cost would far exceed the value it would add. Under the cost approach, the paint and carpet are examples of ___ depreciation, while the foundation issue is ___ depreciation.
choice_a: curable physical deterioration; incurable physical deterioration
choice_b: incurable physical deterioration; curable physical deterioration
choice_c: curable functional obsolescence; incurable functional obsolescence
choice_d: economic obsolescence; curable physical deterioration
explanation: Physical deterioration is curable when the cost to repair an item is less than or equal to the value the repair restores (routine deferred maintenance like paint and flooring), and incurable when the repair cost exceeds the value added or the underlying structural component cannot be practically or economically fixed (a severely cracked foundation).
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2.b (physical deterioration -- curable vs. incurable), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A home includes a lavish, oversized home theater room that cost the original owner $60,000 to build but adds little value for typical buyers, who see it as an overimprovement relative to the neighborhood. Because removing or altering it would cost more than any value gained, this is an example of:
choice_a: Incurable functional obsolescence (a superadequacy)
choice_b: Curable functional obsolescence
choice_c: Economic (external) obsolescence
choice_d: Curable physical deterioration
explanation: A superadequacy is an improvement that exceeds market requirements or preferences; when the cost to remove or cure the overimprovement exceeds any value it would add back, it is classified as incurable functional obsolescence -- distinct from curable functional obsolescence, such as an outdated light fixture that is cheap to replace relative to the value gained.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2.b (functional obsolescence -- curable vs. incurable, superadequacy), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A 40-year-old home that has been meticulously maintained and recently renovated with updated systems throughout may be assigned by an appraiser an effective age that is:
choice_a: Lower than its actual (chronological) age, reflecting its condition and remaining economic life rather than the calendar years since construction
choice_b: Always identical to its actual age, since age is purely a function of the construction date
choice_c: Higher than its actual age in every case involving renovation
choice_d: Irrelevant to the cost approach
explanation: Effective age is the age indicated by a property's condition and utility rather than its actual chronological age; a well-maintained or substantially renovated older home can have an effective age well below its actual age, directly affecting the depreciation an appraiser applies under the cost approach.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2.b (effective age vs. actual/chronological age), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A building has a total economic life of 50 years and an effective age of 15 years. Using the straight-line (age-life) method, what percentage of the building's replacement cost has been lost to accrued depreciation?
explanation: Under the straight-line (age-life) method, accrued depreciation percentage equals effective age divided by total economic life: 15 / 50 = 0.30, or 30% of replacement cost lost to depreciation.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2 (cost approach -- straight-line/age-life depreciation method), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A building's replacement cost new is $260,000. Using the straight-line method, the appraiser determines accrued depreciation of 20%. The underlying land is valued separately at $75,000. What is the appraiser's indicated value via the cost approach?
explanation: Depreciation = $260,000 x 0.20 = $52,000. Depreciated building value = $260,000 - $52,000 = $208,000. Adding land value: $208,000 + $75,000 = $283,000 indicated value under the cost approach.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2 (cost approach -- replacement cost less depreciation plus land value), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An appraiser identifies an outdated kitchen that could be remodeled for $14,000, and market data shows the remodel would increase the home's value by $19,000. From an appraisal standpoint, this functional deficiency is:
choice_a: Curable, because the cost to cure ($14,000) is less than the value it would add ($19,000)
choice_b: Incurable, because $14,000 is a substantial expense in absolute dollar terms
choice_c: Irrelevant to the property's value under any approach
choice_d: Curable only if the current owner agrees to perform the remodel before sale
explanation: A functional deficiency is treated as curable whenever the cost to cure it is less than or equal to the value it restores or adds; here the $14,000 cost is less than the $19,000 value gained, so the deficiency is economically curable and is deducted at cost-to-cure rather than at a larger loss-in-value figure.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2.b (functional obsolescence -- cost to cure), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A comparable sale closed at $310,000. The comparable has an attached garage the subject property lacks (the garage contributes $8,000 of value), and the subject property has a fourth bedroom the comparable lacks (worth $6,000). Applying standard sales comparison adjustment procedure, what is the adjusted value indicated by this comparable?
explanation: Adjustments are made to the comparable to make it match the subject: subtract the value of a feature the comparable has that the subject lacks ($310,000 - $8,000 = $302,000), then add the value of a feature the subject has that the comparable lacks ($302,000 + $6,000 = $308,000 adjusted value).
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.1 (sales comparison approach -- adjustment procedure), Pearson VUE #094401

question: In the sales comparison approach, when a comparable property has a feature the subject property lacks, standard appraisal procedure requires the appraiser to:
choice_a: Adjust the comparable's sale price downward for that feature -- adjustments are always made to the comparable, never to the subject property
choice_b: Adjust the subject property's assumed price upward instead, leaving the comparable's price untouched
choice_c: Ignore the feature difference entirely if it is a minor item
choice_d: Adjust whichever of the two properties happens to have the higher sale price
explanation: The subject property is never adjusted, since it is the property being valued and has no sale price of its own; all dollar or percentage adjustments are applied to each comparable's actual sale price to bring it into line with the subject's characteristics.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.1 (sales comparison approach -- adjustment procedure), Pearson VUE #094401

question: In Texas, an individual completing supervised experience hours toward an appraiser license or certification performs appraisals as a(n):
choice_a: Appraiser trainee, working under the direct supervision of a supervisory (certified or licensed) appraiser, regulated under Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1103 and the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Board (TALCB)
choice_b: Fully independent certified general appraiser from the first day of experience
choice_c: Unlicensed assistant with no state oversight requirement whatsoever
choice_d: TREC-sponsored real estate sales agent performing appraisals as an incidental side activity
explanation: Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1103 establishes appraiser trainee, state licensed, state certified residential, and state certified general categories, all regulated by the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Board (TALCB) -- a separate agency from TREC; a trainee must work under a qualified supervisory appraiser's direct oversight while accumulating experience hours.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1103 (Appraiser Licensing and Certification -- appraiser trainee and TALCB supervision)

question: Under USPAP's Competency Rule, an appraiser who lacks the knowledge or experience necessary to competently complete a specific appraisal assignment must:
choice_a: Either decline the assignment, or disclose the lack of relevant competency to the client and take all steps necessary to complete the assignment competently before accepting it
choice_b: Complete the assignment anyway without disclosing any limitation to the client
choice_c: Delegate the entire assignment to an unlicensed office assistant
choice_d: Simply reduce the appraisal fee to compensate for the gap in expertise
explanation: USPAP's Competency Rule requires an appraiser to possess -- or acquire, through study, association with a qualified appraiser, or other measures -- the competency necessary for a specific assignment, and to disclose any lack of relevant competency to the client before accepting the assignment.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.B.2 (USPAP -- Competency Rule), Pearson VUE #094401

question: USPAP's ethical standards generally prohibit an appraiser from accepting an assignment in which the appraiser's fee is contingent on:
choice_a: The appraiser reaching a predetermined, requested, or otherwise favorable value conclusion
choice_b: The complexity of the property type being appraised
choice_c: The total number of comparable sales analyzed in the report
choice_d: The appraiser's overall years of professional experience
explanation: USPAP's Ethics Rule and appraiser independence standards prohibit fee arrangements contingent on the appraiser reaching a specific, predetermined, or client-desired value conclusion, since such arrangements would compromise the appraiser's objectivity and independence.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.B.2 (USPAP -- appraiser independence, contingent fees), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A thorough Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) prepared by a broker typically incorporates four categories of comparable listings: active listings, pending sales, sold (closed) listings, and:
choice_a: Expired or withdrawn listings, which can indicate overpricing or market resistance
choice_b: Foreclosure auction notices exclusively
choice_c: Off-market pocket listings exclusively
choice_d: New residential construction permits exclusively
explanation: A well-rounded CMA reviews active listings (current competition), pending sales (contracted but not yet closed), sold/closed listings (actual market evidence), and expired or withdrawn listings (properties the market rejected at their asking price), giving a fuller picture of pricing strategy than closed sales alone.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.5 (Comparative Market Analysis -- categories of comparables), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Under Texas Tax Code Section 23.23, once a property qualifies for a residence homestead exemption, the county appraisal district generally may not increase the property's appraised value for tax purposes in a later year by more than:
choice_a: 10% per year over the prior year's appraised value, plus the market value of any new improvements
choice_b: 5% per year, with no exception for new improvements
choice_c: An unlimited amount, strictly tied to current market value each year
choice_d: 20% per year, adjusted annually for inflation
explanation: Texas Tax Code Section 23.23 caps the annual increase in a homestead's appraised value at the lesser of current market value or the prior year's appraised value plus 10% plus the value of new improvements -- a significant Texas-specific taxpayer protection distinct from ordinary market-value appraisal.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.7 (assessed value and tax implications), Pearson VUE #094401; Texas Tax Code Section 23.23 (Limitation on Appraised Value of Residence Homestead)

question: Under Texas Tax Code Section 41.44, a property owner who wishes to protest the county appraisal district's appraised value to the Appraisal Review Board must generally file the written notice of protest by:
choice_a: May 15, or the 30th day after the appraisal district delivered the notice of appraised value, whichever is later
choice_b: December 31 of the tax year, with no earlier deadline
choice_c: Within 10 days of receiving the annual tax bill
choice_d: Any time before the property is sold, with no fixed deadline
explanation: Texas Tax Code Section 41.44 sets the standard protest deadline at May 15 or the 30th day after the appraisal district delivered its notice of appraised value, whichever is later -- missing this deadline generally forfeits the right to protest that year's appraised value before the Appraisal Review Board.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.7 (assessed value and tax implications); Texas Tax Code Section 41.44 (Notice of Protest)

question: An appraisal report is signed and delivered on March 15, but the appraiser was engaged to estimate what the property was worth as of December 31 of the prior year for estate tax purposes. In this situation:
choice_a: The effective date of value (December 31) can properly differ from the date the appraisal report itself was prepared and issued (March 15)
choice_b: The appraisal is automatically invalid because the two dates differ
choice_c: The effective date must always match the date the report is signed
choice_d: USPAP prohibits retrospective (past-dated) appraisal assignments entirely
explanation: The effective date of value is the specific date to which the value opinion applies and can be current, retrospective (a past date, as in an estate or divorce valuation), or prospective (a future date); it is distinct from the report date, which is simply when the appraiser completed and issued the report.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.B.1 (purpose and steps to an appraisal -- effective date of value), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An appraiser estimating a building's reproduction cost by multiplying its total square footage by a current cost-per-square-foot figure derived from similar recent construction is using the:
choice_a: Comparative unit (square-foot) method, the most common and least detailed of the cost-estimating methods
choice_b: Quantity survey method, which itemizes every material quantity and labor cost individually
choice_c: Unit-in-place method, which prices each major building component as installed
choice_d: Income capitalization method
explanation: The comparative unit (square-foot) method is the fastest and most widely used cost-estimating technique, applying a cost-per-square-foot figure to the subject's total area; the quantity survey method is the most detailed and time-consuming (itemizing all materials and labor), while the unit-in-place method falls in between, pricing installed components such as foundations, framing, and roofing.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline III.C.2.c (cost approach -- methods of estimating reproduction/replacement cost), Pearson VUE #094401
